Book Rehana

Capability, responsibility, independence

Most capable people become indispensable by solving problems. They remember everything. They figure things out. They step in. They compensate. They become the person everyone calls.

Eventually, the very capability that made them valuable becomes the thing that keeps everyone else from developing theirs.

I know this because I’ve lived it. I spent much of my life becoming very good at carrying things. Now I’m learning how to build things that can carry themselves.

That question follows me into every room I work in — a business, a household, a young person becoming an adult. Same question. Three different names.

Book Rehana to Speak Keynotes, leadership experiences, workshops

02 The Reframe

Carried. Capable.
The difference is structural.

Most advice about capability is really advice about effort — try harder, care more, show up. This work starts somewhere else: with the structure around a person, not the person’s willpower.

  • A founder without financial clarity isn’t lazy.
  • A teenager without execution experience isn’t unmotivated.
  • A household that runs through one person isn’t dysfunctional.

In each case, something structural is missing — and once it’s built, capability stops being a personality trait and starts being available to anyone.

Stop confusing support with carrying.

03 The Philosophy

Support should create capacity — not dependency.

First

Give people enough structure to practice.

Then

Give them enough context to understand.

Then

Give them enough responsibility to own.

And

Let them become capable.

This isn’t finished work. I still catch myself over-functioning — fixing something myself before asking whether the system should have made that fix unnecessary; writing another checklist before asking whether the checklist builds independence or just moves the dependency around.

I don’t want you to need me every time something changes. I want you to know what to do when it does.

06 The Story

I didn’t set out to build a philosophy about capability.

I was just trying to figure things out — how to make things work, how to solve the problem, how to carry what needed to be carried. For years, I thought I was just good at my jobs.

16+years
7industries
3books

Sixteen years across accounting, audit, international oil and gas operations, software, banking, cybersecurity, and CFO advisory. In every room, I kept doing the same thing without noticing it was unusual: given a piece of the puzzle, I’d go find the rest. Given an incomplete picture, I wouldn’t wait for someone to hand me a finished one.

The better I became at carrying everything, the more everything seemed to require me.

So now I ask one question of everything I build: is this built to need me, or built to work without me?
